context: Stop caching the entrypoint function under the submodule's name. Options: (a) keep the lazy function available but do not write it into globals() under 'main' - return it without caching, so the submodule binding is never clobbered; (b) expose the entrypoint under a distinct name (e.g. cli_main) and keep 'main' meaning the submodule, updating console_scripts and callers; (c) have __getattr__ return the submodule for 'main' and let callers reach the function through it. Prefer whichever keeps the packaging entrypoint stable - check pyproject console_scripts before choosing. Then convert the remaining string-target patches back to the plain form and confirm they still work, since the workaround indirection becomes unnecessary.
description: benchbox/cli/__init__.py __getattr__ handles 'main' by doing 'from benchbox.cli.main import main' and then 'globals()["main"] = main', binding the FUNCTION under the same name as the benchbox.cli.main SUBMODULE. The winner depends on order within a process: importing the submodule first leaves the module bound (Python sets the parent attribute on submodule import); touching the attribute first fires the lazy path and the function overwrites it. Python >= 3.11 masks the consequence because unittest.mock._get_target resolves patch targets via pkgutil.resolve_name, which imports the dotted path so the module wins; Python 3.10 walks the path with getattr and lands on the function. That is why the 2026-07-29 nightly failed on ubuntu-latest/3.10 only, and only for one test - it is order-dependent across xdist workers. Verified against the real package: package-only import followed by attribute access makes 3.10's resolver return <function main> with has get_config_manager=False, matching the nightly error verbatim. PR for nightly-py310-dataframe-options-mock-target worked around it in one test file; this item removes the shadow so every remaining caller is fixed at once.
